claim: Visual speed is believed to be underestimated at low contrast.
source: Visual speed is believed to be underestimated at low contrast, which has been proposed as an explanation of excessive driving speed in fog.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research in the field.

claim: Underestimation of visual speed at low contrast has been proposed as an explanation of excessive driving speed in fog.
source: Visual speed is believed to be underestimated at low contrast, which has been proposed as an explanation of excessive driving speed in fog.
evidence: This is a claim about what has been proposed in the literature.

claim: Speed is underestimated when contrast is reduced uniformly for all objects of the visual scene independently of their distance from the viewer.
source: we confirm that speed is underestimated when contrast is reduced uniformly for all objects of the visual scene independently of their distance from the viewer.
evidence: This is confirmed by experimental data from the study combining psychophysics measurements and driving simulation.

claim: When contrast is reduced more for distant objects, as is the case in real fog, visual speed is actually overestimated.
source: However, we show that when contrast is reduced more for distant objects, as is the case in real fog, visual speed is actually overestimated, prompting drivers to decelerate.
evidence: This is demonstrated through experimental data from psychophysics and driving simulation experiments.

claim: Overestimation of visual speed in fog prompts drivers to decelerate.
source: However, we show that when contrast is reduced more for distant objects, as is the case in real fog, visual speed is actually overestimated, prompting drivers to decelerate.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data from driving simulation experiments showing drivers drove slower in fog conditions.

claim: Perceived speed depends on the spatial distribution of contrast over the visual scene rather than the global level of contrast per se.
source: we demonstrate for the first time that perceived speed depends on the spatial distribution of contrast over the visual scene rather than the global level of contrast per se.
evidence: This is demonstrated through experiments comparing fog and anti-fog conditions with identical global contrast but opposite spatial distributions.

claim: Visual contrast is usually referred to as the difference in brightness between an object and the background.
source: Visual contrast is usually referred to as the difference in brightness between an object and the background (Hofstetter et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Hofstetter et al., 2000.

claim: Classical vision research experiments have shown that the perceived speed of two-dimensional moving objects is underestimated when visual contrast is reduced.
source: These studies have shown that the perceived speed of two-dimensional moving objects—for example, plaid patterns on a computer screen—is underestimated when visual contrast is reduced.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research (Thompson, 1982; Stone and Thompson, 1992; Blakemore and Snowden, 1999; Anstis, 2003).

claim: Recent studies based on driving scenarios have suggested that the underestimation of visual speed at low contrast applies also to perceived self-motion in three-dimensional environments.
source: More recent studies based on driving scenarios have suggested that the underestimation of visual speed at low contrast applies also to perceived self-motion in three-dimensional environments (Snowden et al., 1998; Horswill and Plooy, 2008; Owens et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to driving scenario studies.

claim: In previous studies assessing the effect of visual contrast on motion perception, contrast was reduced uniformly for all objects of the visual scene, irrespective of their distance from the observer.
source: In the abovementioned studies, and more generally in all studies having assessed the effect of visual contrast on motion perception, contrast was reduced uniformly for all objects of the visual scene, irrespective of their distance from the observer.
evidence: This is a characterization of previous research methods based on the cited literature.

claim: Uniform contrast reduction is a valid model to assess the perception of two-dimensional patterns moving on a computer screen.
source: While uniform contrast reduction is a valid model to assess the perception of two-dimensional patterns moving on a computer screen, it is a poor model to investigate how an atmospheric phenomenon like fog affects motion perception in three-dimensional environments.
evidence: This is an inference based on the nature of the experimental paradigm and its appropriateness for different contexts.

claim: Uniform contrast reduction is a poor model to investigate how an atmospheric phenomenon like fog affects motion perception in three-dimensional environments.
source: While uniform contrast reduction is a valid model to assess the perception of two-dimensional patterns moving on a computer screen, it is a poor model to investigate how an atmospheric phenomenon like fog affects motion perception in three-dimensional environments.
evidence: This is an inference based on the physical properties of fog and the experimental findings of the study.

claim: Fog alters visual contrast because tiny water droplets suspended in the air are interposed between the observer and the surrounding objects.
source: Specifically, fog alters visual contrast because tiny water droplets suspended in the air are interposed between the observer and the surrounding objects.
evidence: This is based on established scientific knowledge about the physical properties of fog.

claim: The quantity of water droplets in fog increases along the line-of-sight as distance from the observer increases.
source: The quantity of droplets increases along the line-of-sight as distance from the observer increases.
evidence: This is based on established scientific knowledge about fog physics.

claim: In fog, the contrast of the visual scene decreases with distance.
source: As a consequence, the contrast of the visual scene decreases with distance, and visibility is better for close than for distant objects.
evidence: This is an inference from the physical properties of fog described in the manuscript.

claim: In fog, visibility is better for close than for distant objects.
source: As a consequence, the contrast of the visual scene decreases with distance, and visibility is better for close than for distant objects.
evidence: This is an inference from the physical properties of fog.

claim: The distance-dependent attenuation of contrast experienced in fog is very different from the uniform reduction traditionally adopted in vision research.
source: Therefore, the distance-dependent attenuation of contrast experienced in fog is obviously very different from the uniform reduction traditionally adopted in vision research.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparing the physical properties of fog with experimental methods.

claim: Uniform contrast reduction resembles more closely what one could experience when looking at the environment through a dirty glass or a foggy windshield.
source: Uniform contrast reduction resembles more closely what one could experience when looking at the environment through a dirty glass or a foggy windshield.
evidence: This is an inference based on the nature of uniform contrast reduction.

claim: The effects of distance-dependent contrast reduction on motion perception are unknown (prior to this study).
source: To date, the effects of distance-dependent contrast reduction on motion perception are unknown.
evidence: This is a claim about the state of knowledge in the field prior to the current study.

claim: Twelve experienced drivers were presented with pairs of driving scenes and instructed to estimate which scene moved faster in the first experiment.
source: Twelve experienced drivers were presented with pairs of driving scenes and instructed to estimate which scene moved faster
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure used in the study.

claim: Reducing the contrast of the visual scene altered speed perception with F(4,44) = 28.84, p<0.001, ηG2 = 0.42.
source: Reducing the contrast of the visual scene altered speed perception [F(4,44) = 28.84, p<0.001, ηG2 = 0.42].
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data.

source: As compared to clear visibility (brown dashed line), speed was overestimated with distance-dependent visibility reduction (red bars)
evidence: This is shown in the experimental data and visualized in Figure 3A.

claim: As compared to clear visibility, speed was underestimated with distance-independent visibility reduction (uniform contrast).
source: As compared to clear visibility (brown dashed line), speed was underestimated with distance-independent visibility reduction (green bars).
evidence: This is shown in the experimental data and visualized in Figure 3A.

claim: Reducing visibility affected speed discrimination sensitivity with F(4,44) = 29.58, p<0.001, ηG2 = 0.37.
source: Reducing visibility also affected speed discrimination sensitivity [F(4,44) = 29.58, p<0.001, ηG2 = 0.37]

claim: Participants had more difficulties estimating the driving speed when visibility reduction was independent of distance.
source: This indicates that the participants had more difficulties estimating the driving speed when visibility reduction was independent of distance.

claim: The reduction of speed discrimination sensitivity with distance-independent contrast alteration might result from the fact that distance-independent contrast alteration is seldom encountered in real life.
source: This reduction of speed discrimination sensitivity might result from the fact that distance-independent contrast alteration is seldom encountered in real life.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed data.

claim: Ten experienced drivers who did not participate in the first experiment were instructed to drive at target speeds with either clear or reduced visibility in the second experiment.
source: Ten experienced drivers who did not participate in the first experiment were instructed to drive at target speeds with either clear or reduced visibility.
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure.

claim: Driving speed was affected by the contrast of the visual scene with F(4,36) = 43.18, p<0.001, ηG2 = 0.44.
source: Driving speed was affected by the contrast of the visual scene [F(4,36) = 43.18, p<0.001, ηG2 = 0.44].

claim: As compared to clear visibility, participants drove significantly slower with distance-dependent contrast reduction (fog).

claim: The five visibility conditions differed significantly from one another (p<0.05) in experiment 2.
source: The five visibility conditions differed significantly from one another (p<0.05), and the same pattern was observed for all three target speeds.

claim: The same pattern of results was observed for all three target speeds in experiment 2.
source: The five visibility conditions differed significantly from one another (p<0.05), and the same pattern was observed for all three target speeds.
evidence: This is a result from the experimental data analysis.

claim: Distance-dependent contrast reduction induces an overestimation of visual speed that prompts drivers to drive slower.
source: These behavioural results are consistent with the perceptual results of the first experiment and can be interpreted as follows: distance-dependent contrast reduction induces an overestimation of visual speed that prompts drivers to drive slower
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data from experiments 1 and 2.

claim: Distance-independent contrast reduction evokes an underestimation of visual speed, prompting drivers to drive faster.
source: whereas distance-independent contrast reduction evokes an underestimation of visual speed, prompting drivers to drive faster.

claim: In the experiments, the two types of contrast reduction resulted in the same global attenuation of visual contrast.

claim: The global level of contrast is not the only factor affecting perceived speed.
source: This suggests that the global level of contrast is not the only factor affecting perceived speed.

claim: The spatial distribution of contrast over the visual scene plays a critical role in perceived speed.
source: The spatial distribution of contrast over the visual scene also seems to play a critical role.

claim: In fog, when the driver looks straight ahead, the regions of better visibility in the proximity of the vehicle are typically viewed in peripheral vision.
source: Therefore, when the driver looks straight ahead, the regions of better visibility in the proximity of the vehicle are typically viewed in peripheral vision
evidence: This is an inference based on the properties of fog and typical driving behavior.

claim: In fog, fog acts as a mask obscuring the central region of the visual field.

claim: Speed is underestimated when the peripheral area of the visual field is masked.
source: In particular, we found that speed is overestimated when the central area is occluded, and underestimated when it is the peripheral area that is masked.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work (Pretto et al., 2009).

claim: Speed overestimation in fog could result from the relative contrast between the central and peripheral areas of the visual field.
source: More specifically, speed overestimation in fog could result from the relative contrast between the central and peripheral areas of the visual field.

claim: With anti-fog, visibility was better for distant than for close objects.

claim: Normal fog and anti-fog resulted in opposite spatial distributions of contrast over the visual scene.
source: In other words, normal fog and anti-fog resulted in opposite spatial distributions of contrast over the visual scene, although the global contrast reduction was the same for both fog types.
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: The global contrast reduction was the same for both fog and anti-fog.
source: In other words, normal fog and anti-fog resulted in opposite spatial distributions of contrast over the visual scene, although the global contrast reduction was the same for both fog types.
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: Ten experienced drivers who had not participated in the first two experiments were presented with pairs of driving scenes in the third experiment.
source: Ten experienced drivers who had not participated in the first two experiments were presented with pairs of driving scenes and instructed to estimate which scene moved faster
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure.

source: Visibility affected perceived speed [F(2,18) = 30.01, p<0.001, ηG2 = 0.67].

claim: Previous studies suggested that the speed of visual motion in depth is underestimated when the global level of contrast is reduced.
source: Previous studies suggested that the speed of visual motion in depth is underestimated when the global level of contrast is reduced (Snowden et al., 1998; Horswill and Plooy, 2008; Owens et al., 2010).

claim: An identical global loss of visibility can evoke opposite percepts, depending on the nature of the underlying visual contrast reduction.
source: However, we show that this is only part of the whole picture. In particular, we demonstrate here for the first time that an identical global loss of visibility can evoke opposite percepts, depending on the nature of the underlying visual contrast reduction.
evidence: This is demonstrated through the experimental data comparing fog and anti-fog conditions.

claim: Contrarily to what has been consistently reported in previous studies, a global contrast reduction can also lead to an overestimation of visual speed.
source: Therefore, contrarily to what has been consistently reported in previous studies, a global contrast reduction can also lead to an overestimation of visual speed.
evidence: This is demonstrated through the experimental data showing speed overestimation in fog.

claim: In fog, perceived speed is not determined by the global level of contrast per se, but rather by the spatial distribution of contrast over the visual scene.
source: Our results show that in this situation, perceived speed is not determined by the global level of contrast per se, but rather by the spatial distribution of contrast over the visual scene.

claim: Perceived speed is determined by the relative contrast between the central and peripheral areas of the visual field.
source: More specifically, perceived speed is determined by the relative contrast between the central and peripheral areas of the visual field.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results.

claim: When visibility is better in the peripheral than in the central visual field, as is the case in fog, speed is overestimated.
source: When visibility is better in the peripheral than in the central visual field, as is the case in fog, speed is overestimated.

claim: The visibility gradient plays a critical role in perceived speed.

claim: There is a direct relationship between perceived and produced speed.

claim: Driving speed is strongly affected by perceived visual speed.
source: This demonstrates that driving speed is strongly affected by perceived visual speed.
